record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation affecting the study text; the supplied text includes the report and appendix.
record.tranche_reason: The report evaluates downstream benchmark scores for QWEN models at three parameter sizes. This bears on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not fit loss-scaling laws or make predictions from smaller runs.
record.gate_note: The report states QWEN model sizes and training-token counts, but does not report held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute. The long-context perplexity results vary context-extension techniques and context length, not model size, data, or compute scaling. Rows record QWEN’s own downstream benchmark scores across sizes; scores of other models are not recorded as scaling rows.
record.test_reason: The report supplies downstream scores for its own QWEN models at several scales, bearing on V6's improvement-with-scale component in a new model family. It does not test quantitative predictability. Parameter count and training tokens increase together: 1.8B/2.2T, 7B/2.4T, and 14B/3.0T.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors emphasize competitive base, aligned, coding, and mathematics models against open-source and some proprietary systems. They do not fit or validate a predictive scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Reports benchmark scores across QWEN sizes rather than measuring held-out loss, fitting scaling laws, or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Parameter count is varied across QWEN models; the report evaluates different benchmark tasks and shot settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3 reports perplexity versus inference context length under context-extension techniques.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time context-extension techniques preserve low perplexity beyond the training context length.

record.problems: The QWEN size sweep spans only 1.8B, 7B, and 14B parameters, and the benchmark results have no uncertainty estimates. The results establish monotonic score increases in these tested settings, not predictive accuracy or a scaling law.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row cap was reached. Left out additional disaggregated MMLU and C-Eval category results in Tables 13–14, aligned-model benchmark scores in Table 5, and other results not needed to represent the reported base-model size trend.

untested.parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute over orders of magnitude.
Fitting small runs and predicting larger-run loss.
Fixed-compute optimization and stable parameter/token allocation exponents.
Loss sensitivity to architecture at fixed parameter count; preliminary architecture remarks provide no controlled loss comparison.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes; specialist and aligned-model scores do not establish that form.
Quantitative prediction, out-of-sample validation, relation to pretraining loss, and isolation of parameter scaling from increased training tokens.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices; bending of fitted scaling curves.

missing.what: Tool-use scaling: selection accuracy 92/98/98, input Rouge-L 89/91/93, and false-positive error 19.3/7.3/2.4 for 1.8B/7B/14B. Section 3.4 explicitly discusses saturation.

Code-interpreter scaling, including the exception hidden by aggregate improvement: general executability 8.6/67.2/65.5 versus overall 26.8/70.2/81.7. Final-response math accuracy rises 14.7/41.9/58.4 and visualization accuracy 11.7/47.2/56.4.
Hugging Face Agent scores across 1.8B/7B/14B in run and chat modes; code correctness rises 61.1/71.5/87.0 and 73.2/85.1/95.5 respectively.
Specialist coding size comparisons, including Code-QWEN C++ pass@1 decreasing 20.7 to 18.2 while average rises 30.6 to 38.8; Code-QWEN-Chat average rises 36.1 to 51.9.
Math-QWEN-Chat 7B/14B accuracy: GSM8K 62.5/69.8, MATH 17.2/24.2, Math401 80.8/85.0, Math23K 75.4/78.4.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded numerical scores match their cited tables. The record calls the SocialIQA benchmark 'SIQA' incorrectly as 'SIQA' only if a spelling normalization is needed; Table 17's definitive name is SIQA. Baseline points remain linked because they anchor cross-size comparisons. No uncertainty estimates accompany these trends. The generic rows_left_out phrase about other results does not identify the substantive exceptions in Tables 6–12.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out loss sweep over parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit on small runs and no prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law scaling across the listed other modalities or training regimes.
The report gives benchmark scores across QWEN sizes, but does not fit or validate quantitative predictions, relate scores to pretraining loss, or test a broad scale range.
No comparison of scaling exponents or compute-optimal fits across counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Base QWEN models, jointly increasing parameters and training tokens, across the 20 recorded benchmarks
relationships.reason: Rows r01–r60 show strictly increasing scores at 1.8B, 7B, and 14B on every recorded benchmark; this supports directional improvement only.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased strictly from 1.8B to 7B to 14B on all 20 evaluated benchmarks, establishing a directional trend.

relationships.condition: QWEN-Chat agent task accuracy and specialist coding/math benchmarks, except the qualifications below
relationships.reason: Based on text, with rows missing: Tables 8–9 show increasing task scores, and Tables 10–12 show higher specialist-model scores at 14B on nearly all measures.
relationships.display_finding: Agent task scores increased with size, and 14B specialist models scored higher on nearly all coding and mathematics measures.

relationships.condition: Tool selection, general-purpose code executability, and Code-QWEN C++ synthesis at 7B versus 14B
relationships.reason: Based on text, with rows missing: tool selection stays 98%; general executability falls 67.2% to 65.5%; Code-QWEN C++ pass@1 falls 20.7% to 18.2%, qualifying the broader improvement trend.
relationships.display_finding: Tool selection stayed at 98%, general code executability fell from 67.2% to 65.5%, and Code-QWEN C++ pass@1 fell from 20.7% to 18.2%.
